q: Which statement about ecologically sustainable development (ESD) is debatable?
o: There is a universal definition of ESD
ESD uses, conserves and enhances community resources
ESD aims at better quality of life in the future
n: There is no single universally accepted definition of ecologically sustainable development, so the claim that one exists is the debatable statement. Source: Australia's National Strategy for ESD (1992); Brundtland Report.

q: What is the most common rainwater harvesting method in homes?
n: Roof gutters feeding storage tanks are the most common household rainwater harvesting method. Source: RA 6716 (Rainwater Collector Act); DPWH rainwater harvesting guidelines.

q: Which is a non-renewable energy source?
n: Fossil fuels are non-renewable and finite. They formed over millions of years and cannot be replenished on a human timescale. Source: DOE Philippines; IEA.

q: Which is a renewable energy source?
n: Biomass regrows, so it is a renewable energy source. Source: RA 9513 (Renewable Energy Act of 2008).

q: Which does NOT conform to ESD?
n: Heavy fossil-fuel use raises emissions and depletes resources, contrary to ESD. Source: Brundtland Report; RA 9729 (Climate Change Act).

q: What measures environmental impact in greenhouse gases emitted, usually as CO₂?
n: A carbon footprint measures the greenhouse gases emitted, as CO₂ equivalent. Source: IPCC; GHG Protocol.

q: Basic water harvesting in a residential community.
n: A rainwater (water harvesting) tank is the basic way to harvest water in a residential community. Source: RA 6716; DPWH rainwater harvesting guidelines.

q: What is the water lost from a vegetated surface by evaporation and plant transpiration?
n: Evapotranspiration is water lost from a vegetated surface by evaporation plus plant transpiration. Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56.

q: Which of these energy sources is renewable?
n: Wave and tidal (ocean) energy is renewable. It is driven by the moon's gravity and by wind on the sea, so it is constantly replenished. Source: RA 9513 (Renewable Energy Act).

q: Which US-based rating system scores buildings on energy, water, indoor quality and carbon?
n: LEED, the US Green Building Council's rating system, scores energy, water, indoor environmental quality, materials and carbon. Source: USGBC (usgbc.org).

q: What is also called cradle-to-grave analysis?
n: Life cycle assessment, also called cradle-to-grave analysis, assesses environmental impacts over a product's whole life. Source: ISO 14040.

q: Which evaluation weighs both first cost and recurring maintenance?
n: Life cycle costing weighs first cost against recurring operating and maintenance costs over a building's life. Source: ISO 15686-5; ASTM E917.

q: What means meeting present needs without compromising future generations?
n: Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising future generations. Source: Brundtland Report, Our Common Future (1987).

q: What is a community of living things together with their environment?
n: An ecosystem is a community of living things together with their environment. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, ecosystem.

q: What can decompose under natural conditions?
n: Biodegradable materials decompose under natural conditions. Microorganisms break them down into water, carbon dioxide and biomass. Source: Merriam-Webster; ASTM D6400.

q: Which proactive approach aims to improve existing conditions, not just limit harm?
n: Regenerative design aims to improve existing ecological conditions, not just limit harm. Source: Lyle, Regenerative Design for Sustainable Development.

q: What is a brownfield?
o: A previously developed site with possible contamination
A site with little plant growth
n: A brownfield is a previously developed site that may be contaminated. Source: US EPA, brownfields definition; USGBC LEED.

q: What is the area defined by the perimeter of the building plan?
n: The building footprint is the area defined by the perimeter of the building plan. Source: USGBC LEED Reference Guide (definitions).

q: What flat land beside rivers and streams is likely to flood?
n: A floodplain is flat land beside rivers and streams that is likely to flood. Source: USGBC LEED Reference Guide; FEMA.

q: What is a greenfield?
n: A greenfield is land not previously developed. Building on greenfields consumes farmland or habitat, so green rating systems favour previously developed sites. Source: USGBC LEED Reference Guide (definitions).

q: Which is the preferred location for a green building project?
n: Green buildings prefer brownfield (or previously developed) sites. Redevelopment protects greenfields, floodplains and wetlands. Source: USGBC LEED (Sensitive Land Protection; Brownfield Remediation credits).

q: Which is NOT an alternative-fuel vehicle?
n: Diesel vehicles are conventional. Hydrogen, electric and hybrid vehicles are alternative-fuel. Source: USGBC LEED (Green Vehicles credit); RA 11697 (EVIDA).

q: SRI stands for:
n: SRI means Solar Reflectance Index, which rates how cool a surface stays in sun from its reflectance and emittance. Source: ASTM E1980; USGBC LEED (Heat Island Reduction).

q: Bioswales are mainly for:
n: Bioswales are vegetated channels that slow, filter and infiltrate stormwater runoff, which makes them a stormwater management tool. Source: US EPA, Green Infrastructure; USGBC LEED (Rainwater Management).

q: Which is most pervious?
n: Open-graded gravel without fines has connected voids, so it is the most pervious of the choices. Fine sand clogs the voids, and asphalt and concrete are impervious. Source: US EPA, permeable pavement guidance; ASTM C1701.

q: Native plants that grow reliably with minimal fertilizer and water.
n: LEED defines adaptive plants as natives or well-adapted species that grow reliably with minimal fertilizer, pesticides and water. Source: USGBC LEED Reference Guide (definitions).

q: What is a material's ability to emit heat by radiation?
n: Emissivity is a surface's ability to emit (radiate) absorbed heat. Source: ASTM C1371; USGBC LEED (SRI).

q: What is the loss of soil by wind or flowing water?
n: Erosion is the loss of soil by wind or flowing water. Source: USGBC LEED (Construction Activity Pollution Prevention); Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What is harsh, dazzling light that impairs vision?
n: Glare is harsh, excessive brightness or contrast that causes discomfort or impairs vision. Source: IES Lighting Handbook.

q: What are areas covered fully by impervious materials?
n: Hardscape is areas fully covered by impervious materials: pavement, walks, plazas. Source: USGBC LEED Reference Guide (definitions).

q: What paving is under 50% impervious with plants in its open cells?
n: LEED defines open-grid pavement as paving that is less than 50% impervious, with vegetation in its open cells. Source: USGBC LEED Reference Guide (definitions).

q: What landscaping uses drought-tolerant plants to avoid irrigation?
n: Xeriscaping uses drought-tolerant plants and water-wise design so landscapes need little or no irrigation. Source: Denver Water (origin of the term); USGBC LEED.
